questions.q: What is an optical tweezer, in the context of neutral-atom quantum computing?
options: A tightly focused laser beam used to trap and hold a single neutral atom in place
A physical mechanical clamp that pins an atom to a silicon chip
A superconducting circuit element used to store qubit states
A cryogenic cooling device used to reach millikelvin temperatures
questions.explain: Optical tweezers are focused laser beams that create a region of lower potential energy, trapping individual neutral atoms at precise points -- no mechanical or cryogenic hardware is needed for the trap itself.

questions.q: Why do neutral atoms avoid the stray electric-field sensitivity that can affect charged ions?
options: Because neutral atoms carry no net electric charge, so they don't experience the same long-range electric-field noise that charged particles do
Because neutral atoms are physically larger than ions and therefore immune to all noise
Because neutral atoms do not have electrons at all
Because neutral atoms are always held at absolute zero temperature
questions.explain: Having no net charge means neutral atoms don't respond to stray electric fields the way charged ions can, which is a genuine source of qubit stability specific to this platform.

questions.q: What makes neutral-atom tweezer arrays distinctively reconfigurable compared to platforms with fixed, fabricated traps?
options: Each atom is held by its own independently steerable tweezer beam, so arrays can be arranged in 1D, 2D, or more complex patterns and even rearranged mid-computation
Fixed, fabricated-trap platforms are actually more reconfigurable than neutral-atom arrays
Reconfigurability has nothing to do with how the atoms are trapped and is purely a software feature unrelated to the hardware
Neutral atoms can only ever be arranged in a single fixed 1D line with no exceptions
questions.explain: Because tweezers are independently steerable laser beams rather than fixed physical structures, the array's geometry and even atom positions during computation can be adapted, unlike a fabrication-time-fixed trap layout.

questions.q: What is a Rydberg state, and why is it central to creating entanglement between neutral atoms?
options: A state used only to cool the atom closer to absolute zero
The default ground state that every neutral-atom qubit sits in when idle
A state in which the atom loses its electron entirely and becomes a bare ion
An electronic state where one electron is excited to a very high energy level, greatly increasing the atom's effective size and enabling strong, controllable interactions with nearby Rydberg atoms
questions.explain: Rydberg states dramatically increase an atom's effective size and create strong, distance-dependent interactions between nearby excited atoms -- the mechanism harnessed for entangling gates, not a cooling or idle state.

options: The effect where one atom already excited to a Rydberg state prevents a second nearby atom from also being excited to that same state, due to their strong mutual interaction
A failure mode where atoms are permanently lost from the trap
A physical barrier placed between tweezer beams to prevent atoms from colliding
The process of cooling atoms down before they are loaded into tweezers
questions.explain: Rydberg blockade is the controllable, distance-dependent interaction where a nearby already-excited atom blocks a second atom from reaching the same Rydberg state -- this is the mechanism used to implement entangling gates, not a hardware barrier or loss mechanism.
